source.title: Unlearning or Obfuscating? Jogging the Memory of Unlearned LLMs via Benign Relearning
source.authors: Shengyuan Hu; Yi-Wei Fu; Steven Z. Wu; Virginia Smith

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign fine-tuning can restore harmful answers, using a different setting and evaluation from the claim: relearning on models that have undergone machine unlearning, measured by answer relevance rather than refusal rates.
record.gate_note: The paper's WMDP experiments report harmful-question answer-quality results after benign relearning, which bear on V2. They do not measure refusal rates or test safety-trained models' response-opening tokens, suffixes, decoding, or safety-localized weights. Results on TOFU, Harry Potter memorization, and the synthetic name-pair task concern other targets and are not rows for these claim versions. The paper cites prior work on benign fine-tuning and safety, but reports no results from that work.
record.test_reason: The study measures whether benign, topic-related fine-tuning restores knowledge that machine unlearning suppressed. It does not measure whether a safety-trained model's refusal or harmful compliance erodes. Three points rule out V2. First, the subjects are unlearned models, not refusal-trained ones; Llama-3-8b is the base model, not the Instruct version. Second, the original Zephyr already answers the WMDP questions (score 5.92), so there is no refusal to erode. Third, the measure is answer quality on hazardous questions, i.e. recovery of knowledge or capability. This is a related but different construct, so the finding goes under fits_no_version. The paper mentions Qi et al. (2023) on benign fine-tuning compromising safety only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that finetuning-based approximate unlearning obfuscates outputs rather than removing knowledge. Small, loosely related or public relearn sets recover unlearned content across WMDP, TOFU and WHP, with recovery dependent on how closely the relearn data relates to the unlearned data. They urge caution, more robust unlearning methods, and evaluations beyond forget/retain query completion.
record.recipe_differences: This is a benign-relearning attack on models after machine unlearning, not the original safety fine-tuning intervention or first-token KL analysis. Relearning uses related public information or a subset of unlearning data and evaluates recovery of knowledge.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies with unlearning method and model; the authors also report dependence on relearn-data relevance, amount of relearning, evaluation task, and (for RMU) knowledge of the corrupted layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on benign, topic-related public text restores unlearned hazardous WMDP knowledge to near pre-unlearning quality. This holds across GA, GD, KL, NPO and SCRUB on Zephyr and Llama-3-8b, and is stronger after LoRA unlearning. Gibberish relearn text does not restore WMDP MCQ accuracy (25.05% vs 24.67% with no relearning). RMU recovers on MCQ but little on answer completion unless the corrupted layer is zero-initialized.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Approximate (gradient-based) unlearning of hazardous knowledge is shallow: a small amount of benign, related fine-tuning data restores the suppressed knowledge.

record.problems: The WMDP answer-quality evaluation uses an LLM judge and an evaluation set of 70 questions; relearn data is generated or selected to be related to the queries, so the results do not establish that generic benign instruction data increases refusal-based harmful compliance. The paper notes that evaluation metrics can give an incomplete picture and that relearning effectiveness depends on the task and unlearning method. Several Figure 4 values are available only in the plot.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for TOFU or Harry Potter keyword/text recovery, synthetic name-pair recovery, retain-set MT-Bench results, or RMU MCQ and answer-completion results: these do not measure harmful user-request compliance as named in V2. The paper's separate WMDP MCQ accuracy variation by relearn text (Appendix C.5.5, Table 7) is also omitted because it measures MCQ accuracy rather than harmful answer generation.

untested.parts: No safety-trained model's refusal or harmful-compliance rate is measured before and after benign fine-tuning.
No harmful-data fine-tuning of aligned models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No safety-localization test. The RMU layer-knowledge result concerns unlearning, not safety.
Section 5 argues token-level unlearning losses leave associations intact, but this concerns unlearning, not safety alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the WMDP rows to V2, but the paper studies unlearning robustness, not safety alignment. The baseline model (Zephyr) already gives hazardous answers (5.92), and one model is a base Llama-3-8b. Figure 4 values are partly legible in the extracted text, but their mapping to methods is ambiguous. The capability-recovery finding could inform a separate claim about shallow unlearning.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune safety-trained models on harmful examples or measure refusal removal.

Tests benign relearning on unlearned models and scores answers to harmful WMDP questions, not refusal rates in safety-trained models generally; the relearn data is targeted and related to the questions rather than ordinary benign instruction data.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Discusses why unlearning may leave associations intact, but does not test why safety training would be shallow.
Does not test training to spread safety beyond initial response tokens or its robustness.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: WMDP harmful-question completion after benign public relearning on Zephyr and Llama-3
reader_labels.reason: Answer-quality scores rise after benign relearning across the reported full-model methods and Zephyr LoRA methods (r1–r14); the paper says relearned WMDP answers are substantially better and close to pre-unlearning quality.
